newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Shooting in Central Africa after march, 15 wounded.
newsitem.headline: Shooting in Central Africa after march, 15 wounded.

text.p: Troops loyal to Central African Republic President Ange-Felix Patasse and mutinous soldiers exchanged fire in the capital on Monday after a march by civilians demanding Patasse's resignation, witnesses said.
Interior Minister Jean Willybiro-Sacko told Reuters 12 members of the security forces and three civilians were wounded in clashes following the break-up of the protest.
Some witnesses and the rebels spoke of up to four deaths. The government formally denied the reports. There was no independent confirmation either way.
The impoverished Central African nation is in the grip of its third army mutiny of the year. Four African leaders sent by a Franco-African summit negotiated a truce earlier this month.
The shooting broke out about a km (half a mile) from the city centre as or after the march involving several thousand people dispersed, according to differing versions of events.
Some witnesses said security forces broke up the march, which began in populous districts controlled by the mutineers. Others accused loyalists of firing at the marchers.
Government spokesman Theophile Ndouba told state radio that mutineers had attacked government forces under cover of the march "so as to indulge in looting".
A rebel spokesman told a private radio station the rebels had taken prisoner a police academy director.
A precarious calm later returned to the capital.
French troops who are stationed in Bangui and who intervened in May under a defence pact to keep Patasse in power were not drawn into Monday's incidents, the witnesses said.
A spokesman for the African mediating team, Gabonese Colonel Ibaba Alioune, told Reuters they were investigating.
The mutinies, which began in April, were initially over pay but developed into demands, backed by the opposition, that Patasse step down. The latest revolt began in mid-November.
Patasse, elected 1993, has dismissed the demands as unconstitutional. The mutiny has turned into bloody feuding between his Baya tribe and Yakomas who dominate rebel ranks.
Mutineers control suburbs of the capital while loyalists and French troops control the centre.
The two sides on December 22 extended for one month a ceasefire and agreed to form a joint security commission.

The accord was signed by Patasse, rebel leader Captain Anicet Saulet, mediator General Amadou Toumani Toure, the former military ruler of Mali, and French ambassador Jean-Marc Simon, who took part in the negotiations.
